chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Aging World — Japan, China and Developed Markets

lessons.title: China's Demographic Cliff: The End of the One-Child Dividend

children.text: Japan aged because it got rich, a slow, income-driven slide familiar to almost every developed economy. China is aging faster than any large economy in recorded history, and for a very different reason: a large part of it was designed by policy, not earned by decades of rising income. That distinction is the whole story of this lesson.

China's fertility rate was already falling through the 1970s, under an earlier 'later, longer, fewer' campaign encouraging later marriage and smaller families. The one-child policy, introduced in 1980 out of concern that rapid population growth would outrun the country's resources, compressed that decline far faster and far further than income growth alone would have. Most countries take generations to move from a large family norm to a small one. China did it in roughly one generation, by law.

body.title: From One Child to Begging for Three

events.title: One-child policy introduced
events.description: Most urban couples are restricted to one child, with exceptions in rural areas and for some ethnic minorities, enforced through fines, incentives, and in some periods, coercive measures.

events.title: One-child policy officially ends
events.description: China announces the end of the policy after 35 years, citing the need to address a rapidly aging population and shrinking workforce.

events.title: Universal two-child policy takes effect
events.description: All couples are permitted two children, but the anticipated baby boom largely fails to materialise, as costs of housing, education, and childcare had already reset family expectations.

events.title: Three-child policy and removal of birth limits
events.description: China raises the limit to three children and removes most remaining family planning fines and restrictions, alongside new subsidies in various cities, still with limited effect on the birth rate.

events.title: Population declines for the first time since 1961
events.description: China's population falls by roughly 850,000, the first annual decline since the famine years following the Great Leap Forward, over six decades earlier.

body.text: The one-child policy's most visible unintended consequence was a severe sex ratio imbalance, driven by son preference combined with the spread of ultrasound technology enabling sex-selective abortion. Decades of a skewed sex ratio at birth have left China with an estimated surplus of tens of millions more men than women of marriageable age, a demographic legacy with its own social and economic consequences that will likely persist for decades.

children.text: Demographers describe the one-child generation's family structure with a simple shorthand: 4-2-1. Four grandparents and two parents, all potentially depending, financially and for eldercare, on a single adult child. This is a very different household economics problem from Japan's, where family sizes fell more gradually and eldercare burdens are more evenly spread across siblings. In China, an entire generation is being asked to fund the retirement of up to six family members with the earnings and savings of one working adult.

body.label: The 4-2-1 Family Structure
body.context: Four grandparents and two parents potentially relying on one only child, a direct demographic legacy of the one-child policy

children.text: Speed of Aging: Faster Than Any Major Economy

Demographers often measure how fast a country ages by the years it takes to move from an 'aging society', where 7% of the population is 65 or older, to an 'aged society', where that share hits 14%. France, aging gradually alongside its own economic development, took roughly a century to make that jump. Japan, already the fastest major economy to age, did it in about a quarter of that time. China's pace is on track to be similarly fast, or faster, compressed into scarcely a generation by the one-child policy's abrupt effect on births.

body.text: The birth counts, population change, sex ratio, and pace-of-aging figures in this lesson are rounded, illustrative approximations drawn from widely cited Chinese government and academic sources, meant to teach the underlying framework rather than serve as precise reference data. Verify exact figures from China's National Bureau of Statistics or UN World Population Prospects before citing them elsewhere.

children.text: Economic Consequences: Losing the Factory of the World's Cheapest Labour

China's rise as the world's manufacturing hub was built substantially on an abundant, cheap, working-age labour force. As that pool shrinks and wages rise, the cost advantage that drew decades of export manufacturing to Chinese coastal provinces has been eroding. This is one of the structural forces, alongside geopolitics and trade policy, behind the 'China Plus One' shift of manufacturing capacity toward Vietnam, Mexico, and India, a trend covered in more depth from an investing angle later in this course's discussion of sector implications.

body.text: A shrinking, aging workforce also strains the pension system funding it. A widely cited 2019 projection from the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences estimated that China's main urban pension fund could be depleted by around 2035 under then-current trends, absent reform. Actual outcomes depend heavily on policy responses since then, but the direction of the pressure, more retirees, fewer contributing workers, is not in question.

children.text: The Policy U-Turn Has Not Worked, Yet

cells: One-child policy ends; universal two-child policy begins
A brief, modest uptick in births, followed by a resumed decline as underlying costs of raising children remained high
Three-child policy and removal of most birth limits and fines
Births continued falling through 2022 and 2023, reaching record lows
Various city and provincial-level cash subsidies, tax breaks, extended parental leave
Effects have so far been localised and modest; national birth numbers have not reversed

children.text: This pattern, removing restrictions but not seeing birth rates recover, is not unique to China. It shows that once a society's expectations around family size, career timing, and the cost of raising children reset to a lower level, reversing course through policy alone is far harder than the original restriction was to enforce. This matters directly for how much weight investors should place on any future Chinese pro-natalist stimulus as a growth catalyst.

body.title: Quick Check: Policy-Driven vs Income-Driven Aging
body.question: What is the key structural difference this lesson draws between Japan's aging and China's aging?
options: There is no meaningful difference; both aged for identical reasons
Japan aged primarily through gradual, income-driven fertility decline, while China's decline was substantially compressed and accelerated by the one-child policy
China aged only because of emigration, not falling births
Japan's aging was policy-driven, while China's was purely income-driven
body.explanation: Japan's fertility decline tracked the slower, more typical pattern of rising income, urbanization, and social change seen across developed economies. China's one-child policy compressed a similar transition into roughly one generation by law, producing a faster and more abrupt aging curve, along with side effects like the sex ratio imbalance that a purely income-driven transition would be far less likely to produce at the same scale.

body.title: Reading a Pro-Natalist Headline
body.scenario: A news headline reads: 'China announces new nationwide cash bonus for every second and third child, effective next year.' A colleague suggests this could meaningfully boost China's consumer-facing sectors, baby products, education, and housing, within two to three years.
body.prompt: Based on this lesson, how would you respond to that expectation?
body.modelAnswer: Be skeptical of a fast, large effect. This lesson showed that China's earlier policy relaxations, ending the one-child policy in 2015, the two-child policy in 2016, and the three-child policy with removed fines in 2021, each produced only brief or localised upticks in births, not a sustained reversal. Once a society's expectations around family size and the cost of raising children reset lower, subsidies alone have historically struggled to change that trajectory quickly. A more measured expectation would be a modest, uncertain effect at best, worth monitoring in the data over several years rather than pricing in in a rebound.

body.text: China did not simply age. It engineered a faster fertility decline than almost any country in history, then discovered that the policy lever it used to push fertility down does not work nearly as well in reverse.

points: China's one-child policy (1980 to 2015) compressed a typically multi-generational fertility decline into roughly one generation, producing a faster and more abrupt aging curve than Japan's income-driven decline.
China's population declined in 2022 for the first time since 1961, and 2023 births fell to a record low since 1949, despite the policy having ended years earlier.
The policy's unintended consequences include a severe sex ratio imbalance and the '4-2-1' family structure, where one working adult can face financial responsibility for up to six family members.
China is aging roughly as fast as Japan did, and dramatically faster than France, in terms of years taken to move from a 7% to a 14% elderly population share.

China's shrinking, aging, and increasingly expensive labour force is one structural driver behind the 'China Plus One' manufacturing shift, and its pro-natalist policy reversals since 2015 have so far failed to meaningfully lift the birth rate.
